notes.text: In both the senses "to loosen" and "to permit" the antonym is Ɂsr vb. Note that the otherwise common usage of the pael as "to begin" is not found in JBA where it has been replaced by the Hebraism אתחל. In the sense of "to dwell", the context is generally that of temporary or nomadic residence as opposed to more permanent residence as expressed with ytb and dwr.

notes.text: The LS2-suggested Syriac vocalization as šakkīḇ must be seen as uncertain, as is the JBA vocalization: the Yemenite tradition has škiyb . Note the vocalization of the Syriac of škybw "death" with initial shwa. Logically, one might expect the reverse, since death is rather permanent whereas sleeping is not. The majority of Syriac p.p.-based adjectives have moved to geminated middle radical forms, however. In most such cases, one should assume that both forms were used in early times.

Hence the active participle in mem, already in OfA, which even shows the distinctive heh of the early h/afel. CPA shows a perfect passive ܐܫܟܝܚ ; Sam. almost always שקח or שקע: Mand. T-stem as if true ettafal; LJLA regularly shows initial heh in perfect forms of the T-stem, reflecting the BA form.

notes.text: In all dialects this lexeme can be used for "sending word," but in many it is properly kept distinct from terms for sending people or goods; see s.vv. yšr and šdr. In some Palestinian texts and LJLA the pael is also used for simple sending, as shown in the citations, but the note in DJPA suggesting that all exxs. in PTA and Gal. are paels takes things too far, and indeed he misunderstands the function of pael in this verb. The examples he cites of vocalized forms in PTA are of the pael because they mean "to release" not because they mean "to send." In the simple meaning, all unvocalized forms must thus be taken to be of G and Gt. While it is impossible to disambiguate between possible Gt and Dt forms in the former dialects, the literary dialects in contrast (i.e. JLA, Syr) clearly have only Gt for "to be sent on a mission". In later dialects "stretching out the hand" is expressed with yšṭ C.

notes.text: Note the unusual passive form יתשמע at Sf A1; possibly an early example if ittaf'al. We have here listed the G p.p. construction as a separate gloss because with this verb it is by for the most common such construction, albeit a grammatical one rather than a lexical peculiarity, and because it has been the subject of some discussion. E.Y. Kutscher, in "Two 'Passive' Constructions..." (1969) argued that this construction was borrowed from Old Persian. Several more recent scholars, however, have realized that it is simply an example of the the middle stage of the common Semitic and Indo-European linguistic drift passive > perfect > preterite.
